newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor signs $2.4 billion budget.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor signs $2.4 billion budget.

text.p: Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles on Tuesday said he had signed the state's $2.4 billion budget for fiscal 1998, which began Tuesday.
The budget imposes a $66 million reduction from the previous year's total, Knowles said at a ceremony Tuesday.
The Democratic governor and leaders of the Republican-controlled legislature clashed earlier this year on the proper degrees of cuts to government agencies.
Republicans generally proposed deeper cuts than Knowles and other Democrats wanted.

Knowles said the resulting compromise, struck in May, will result in some obvious service reductions. He cited environmental protection, fish and wildlife management and public safety as vulnerable state functions.
"We do have some concerns about maintaining the services that we have," he said.
Nonetheless, he said, continued budget cuts will be needed to help the state cope with the state's declining oil production.
Four of every five dollars in the state's general budget come from North Slope oil royalties, taxes and fees; production there has declined since the 1988 peak of 2 million barrels a day.
Budget measures approved by Knowles also included a $700 million transfer within the Alaska Permanent Fund, the 20-year-old trust fund set up with state oil revenues.
The legislation, which got bipartisan support, transfers money from the trust fund's earnings reserve account to its hard-to-tap principal.

The Permanent Fund principal may not be spent without a vote of approval from the Alaska public, but politicians may spend money from the earnings reserve with a majority vote in the state legislature.
The fund's assets now total nearly $23 billion -- an amount that, if measured in $1 bills, "would measure up to Mount McKinley 387 times," Knowles said.

Even counting the annual Permanent Fund dividend, which has topped $1,000 in recent years and is paid to almost every state resident, state spending in the coming fiscal year will be $340 less per capita than it was in 1979, Knowles said.
For the end of fiscal 1997, the state reaped an estimated $62 million surplus, thanks to high oil prices and investment windfalls, he said.
Alaska has no personal income tax and no state sales tax.
